newsitem.title: JAPAN: Japan's June trade surplus up but below forecasts.
newsitem.headline: Japan's June trade surplus up but below forecasts.

text.p: Japan's contentious trade surplus grew for the third consecutive month in June, reinforcing fears of renewed trade friction with the United States but boosting the dollar as the latest rise came in below expectations.

The June trade surplus rose 27.7 percent from a year earlier to 934.21 billion yen ($8.05 billion), the Finance Ministry said Thursday. The customs-cleared trade surplus with the United States, often a source of bilateral tension, also grew 26.8 percent in June from a year earlier to 373.14 billion yen ($3.21 billion).
The figures were not adjusted for seasonal factors.
The figures were slightly below economists' forecasts, which ranged from 971.0 billion yen ($8.37 billion) to 1.61 trillion yen ($13.8 billion) for the overall surplus.

Upon seeing that the surplus was smaller than expected, currency dealers quickly moved to snatch up dollars, sending the greenback above 116 yen, up from around 115.50 yen before the release of the data.
"The dollar was bought (for yen) as the June surplus was at the lower end of projections," said Toshihiko Masaki, senior trader at Long-Term Credit Bank of Japan.

Although Japan has said that Tokyo and Washington have no intention of using exchange rates as a trade tool, currency traders surmise that in order to rectify the imbalance, the two governments would need to push up the value of the yen.
A strong yen makes Japanese goods more expensive in global markets and makes them less competitive for export.

"Japan-U.S. trade tension is now being temporarily shelved by the market," Masaki said. But he added that traders may switch their focus back to trade issues within the next few months if the United States puts the heat on Japan over the surplus.
Japanese officials stressed that the recent rise in the trade surplus was due to special factors.
"The reason for the drastic increase in the trade surplus from a year ago in the April-June period is from the special factor of the consumption tax increase," said a finance ministry official.
Japan raised its consumption tax to 5 percent from 3 percent on April 1. The measure was followed by a drop in private consumption, leading to a decrease of imports, economists said.
But the ministry official added that he could not make any predictions on when the effect of the tax rise would end.
Economists also said it was still premature to assume the surplus had hit its peak.
In the April-June quarter, Tokyo posted a trade surplus of 2.48 trillion yen ($21.3 billion), nearly double the figure from the previous year, jumping by 94.3 percent.

"What we are looking at is the difference between export and import growth. Exports are still growing quite a bit faster than imports and we think the surplus will continue to increase for some months to come," said Richard Jerram, chief economist at ING Barings Securities in Tokyo.
In June, exports rose 12.5 percent from a year ago while imports managed to grow by 8.7 percent.
Economists said the yen's weakening earlier in May has continued to support exports while capping imports.
"It's clear that the depreciation of the yen over the last two years is having an impact on the competitiveness of imports and exports," said ING's Jerram.
In June, imports of cars to Japan dropped 24.1 percent from a year ago, while Tokyo's car exports jumped by 39.4 percent.

Although Japanese officials have stressed that the surplus in the trade of goods and services will not increase significantly and invite trade friction, signs were evident that there were growing concerns among Tokyo's trade partners.

"The U.S. administration understands that the growing trade surplus in Japan has the potential of increasing trade friction with Japan," said Andrew Card, president of the American Automobile Manufacturers' Association.
Card told Reuters Financial Television that the recent big surge in Japanese auto exports to the United States was a result of the excessively weak yen.
Thursday's data also showed that Tokyo's trade surplus with the United States jumped 48.8 percent in the first six months of this year compared with the same period a year earlier.
